newsitem.title: FRANCE: ALPINE SKIING-FRITZ STROBL LEADS AUSTRIAN CLEAN SWEEP.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-FRITZ STROBL LEADS AUSTRIAN CLEAN SWEEP.

text.p: Unheralded Fritz Strobl led Austria to an impressive clean sweep in the first downhill of the men's Alpine skiing World Cup season on Sunday.

The 24-year-old military policeman from Steinfeld, winner ot the super-G European Cup last season, pipped compatriot Werner Franz by 0.02 seconds and world champion Patrick Ortlieb by 0.11 seconds with a time of 1:51.61.
Fellow Austrian and namesake Josef Strobl, the surprise 1994 winner here, was fourth on 1:51.81. The two Strobls are not related.
The Austrian success confirmed their fine showing in the first and only training run of the season, held here on Thursday, in which they clocked the six fastest times.
In 1994, the Austrians also took the first four places of a World Cup downhill here.
With such a strong squad, they look set to be a tough challenge for downhill World Cup holder Luc Alphand of France, who won here last year.

This time, the 31-year-old Frenchman had to be content with sixth place in 1:51.90, one hundredth of a second behind Italy's Kristian Ghedina, who beat him for second place at the world championships in Sierra Nevada last winter.

Despite his country's outstanding performance, the result was a disappointment for Ortlieb, who had said he had dreamed of winning on the other side of the mountain on which he became Olympic champion in 1992.

Franz, who like Strobl comes from the Kaernten region made famous by downhill legend Franz Klammer, must have been frustrated as well, as he looked ideally placed to score his first World Cup victory after two second places in Val Gardena in 1993 and in Wengen last year.

But Strobl, whose highest World Cup placing was 16th in a super-G last season in Lillehammer and who started with number 43, took advantage of the impeccable conditions to cause the first upset of the men's season.
Sunny, dry and cold weather made the OK piste the perfect setting for the start of the downhill season which had been twice delayed because of bad weather.

The opening race, scheduled for Whistler, Canada, eight days ago, was called off because of snowfalls and the Val d'Isere race had to be halted after 17 starters on Saturday because of poor visibility at the top of the piste.
Sunday's downhill was interrupted for 10 minutes after Canadian Graydon Oldfield fell.

Olympic champion Tommy Moe of the U.S., starting behind Oldfield, was flagged to a stop after he had clocked the fastest intermediate time. He was allowed to go back to the top and start again but finished two seconds off the pace.
